A bunch of misc. recs:

* Skinamarink (2022) -- Lofi/analog horror film that has strong evil/negative vibes. Not everyone's cup of tea due to the pacing gimmick.
* Mandy (2018) -- First half is a bit more ethereal than evil. Second half is nasty.
* Evil Dead (1981) -- Bitter and happy about it. Deliberately rubs your face in the muck.
* When Evil Lurks (2023) -- Gritty, pessimistic horror film about evil reclaiming the earth.
* Belladonna of Sadness (1973) -- Maybe a bit atypical for what you're looking for but something about it oozes evilness.
* Mad God (2021) -- One of the most mean-spirited animated movies I've ever seen
* We Need to Talk About Kevin (2011) -- More explicitly dramatic than the others but Kevin is... evil. And no one wants to talk about it.

It's a little obvious but I thought the overall vibe of *Evil Dead Rise* was amazing for conjuring this real-world place that just oozed corruption and awfulness. 

Pretty much anything by Gaspar Noe, no matter how seemingly light-hearted the material, just feels... "off" in a way that's hard to describe. Even when he's not using music literally designed to make the audience nauseous, like at the beginning of *Irreversible*.

This is going to sound like a weird one but the recent *Piranha* also made me feel just on edge and awful the whole way through. It's all very colourful and "funny" but there's a nihilist, nearly existential, almost Lovecraftian underbelly showing how we're all just meat. The scenes of beautiful people getting ripped apart are so visceral, especially since the horrors take place in the middle of the day. I just felt so fucked up afterwards.

The Witch (2015) is a perfectly example in my opinion. It's literally about an evil power tearing a family apart, but what sets it apart from other horror movies is that 17th century New England setting that makes that story so believable for the characters. The sense of dread is thick throughout the film, slowly building to these little bursts of disturbing imagery. It's use of sound and music is exceptional too.

How about The Witch? A family battling a force that has them completely outmatched and ensnared, and is just toying with them before killing them one by one.

The White Ribbon? (And I suspect this isn't only Haneke film that belongs in this category.)

Also, I'm not sure that Don't Look Now belongs here. It's tragic, but I don't feel that it's *evil*. There are moments in the film where light shines through (most obviously the sex scene) and even at the very end where the protagonist in dying there's a sense that you're seeing a life in its totality, in a mood of acceptance or sympathy rather than horror.
Funny Games (and Caché to a certain degree, also by Haneke) is incredibly negative. I won’t spoil the film if you haven’t seen it, but it’s designed to mess with your head in that way.

I like the vibe of [The Endless](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3986820)... It's not a perfect movie but they do successfully convey the sense of there being a corner of the world where the normal laws of time and space don't apply, that the audience doesn't or even can't know enough to understand or contend with what makes that place different. It's not classical evil in the sense of an active malevolence contrary to human interests, more of an incomprehensible cosmic indifference that to me is even scarier. I think the ending undermines the setup somewhat, but it's still memorable.

There's a similar energy going on in [Annihilation](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2798920). It has some good "wow" moments and some really disturbing imagery, but like The Endless I think it didn't quite follow through how I hoped after reading the novel it was based on.

The Seventh Continent is the most evil feeling movie I’ve ever seen. By Haneke

The White Ribbon is a great recommendation. Haneke is a master at this vibe. Specifically The Seventh Continent takes it to another level, it’s one of the few films I would suggest a trigger warning for.

*The Ring*, *Sinister*, *Cure*, and *Pulse* — the curse subgenre of horror? — are exceptionally effective in this way, kind of putting the viewer right into the middle of the phenomena. They're structured to be self-similar to what they're about. There's a cool thing in that they're essentially over before they even start; the protagonist doesn't stand a chance, they're up against something they can never understand much less combat or even escape. You aren't surprised when it isn't a happy ending. Funhouse mirror movies. There's probably many more examples I haven't seen yet. 

*The Ring*, technically a happy ending but the cost is so extraordinarily high!

*Insidious* the dude chooses to move to the house before the film starts and once he's there it's way too late, he's already imprisoned by his own illusion of becoming famous writing about scary houses. He flails about a little while as the bad thing messes with him and that's the whole movie. A scary movie about scary movies. 

*Pulse* even the viewer has no idea what's going on — you get cursed too!

*Cure* the detective makes it to the half way point in this one, but he still doesn't stand a chance because it's his actual day job as a cop to get to the bottom of this thing that's impossible to get to the bottom of. The movie about hypnotism very effectively hypnotizes you!

Miss Violence (2013) -  an arthouse film similar to Dogtooth. A rather nihilistic watch both in terms of content and cultural meta. Seems to be part of a Greek trend of festival films put out to be, some say, provocative on purpose. Still, I consider it a really great film but YMMV.

River's Edge (2018) - A Japanese film that has a very heavy dark aura running throughout. It's hard to describe but some scenes are pitch jet-black nihilistic held up further by a foreboding soundtrack. It's a slow burn but definitely one of the darkest films I've watched in terms of tone and ending.

Super Dark Times (2017) - If you like River's Edge (I did) and Blackcoat's Daughter (it was ok), you will enjoy this. From the opening shot alone you can already tell something sick is gonna happen in this story and the entire time the film's atmosphere just adds to the growing dread. While I won't say who the real antagonist is, I will say they're meant to evade all accusations.

Hour of the Wolf (1968) - Bergman's first and only foray into the horror genre. Much less scary as it is psychological (hence, Bergman.) Was released shortly after Persona and might be considered the "Shadow" movie to Persona's id versus ego dialectic.

Carnival of Souls (1962) - Inspired by Bergman and the director's only film. Like above, don't expect anything scary but more of a psychological tone that reminded my of Rosemary's Baby in a way.

I’m gonna have to disagree with *Come and See*. The events shown in the film are evil, but the film itself is a condemnation of what it depicts. Flyora is put through hell, but the audience is not expected to revel in his misery. In the end the message is pretty effectively anti-war. 

A better example would be something like *Funny Games*, where not only are we made to watch a very disturbing series of events, but also frequently reminded that this is exactly what we signed up for and were hoping to see. The horror and the violence is not intended to be cautionary; rather it’s presented as a sick form of entertainment for the villains and for the audience. Actually, you might even say that it is being *inflicted* upon the audience just as it is being inflicted upon the victims in the movie. We see this especially in the scene where on of them manages to grab a gun and shoot one of the antagonists, only for the other one to pick up a TB remote and *rewind the movie itself* as if to say “You thought we’d let you off that easy?” I think that’s what makes it such a brilliant horror film - Haneke is not merely toying with the characters in the film, but with the audience, too. There have been plenty of other horror movies before and since that have done the “holding up a mirror to the audience” schtick, but none have done so quite as effectively, or in such an interactive fashion. 

I think that’s what makes *Funny Games* an “evil” film. It’s almost malicious in its intent to disturb anyone who watches it. *Come and See* is also meant to be disturbing, but for a very different and far more noble purpose. That’s why I would never call it evil.

If you're ok with docudramas as well, I'd say that some of the later mondo films by Gualtiero Jacopetti and Franco Prosperi are actually downright evil. *Africa Addio* (1966) is beautifully filmed, scored, and edited, but its telling of African decolonization is so awfully dehumanizing that it comes out almost like a defence of either perpetuated European colonization or apartheid. There's also controversy as to whether Jacopetti and Prosperi intervened in a court martial so they could film the defendant being executed.

Their follow-up *Goodbye Uncle Tom* (1971) is even worse because it's so disgustingly nauseating in how it takes pleasure in showing enslaved Africans being brutalized and humiliated by slavers--and the worst part is that the extras playing those enslaved Africans were pretty much corvee forced labourers supplied to the filmmakers by actual dictator Papa Doc Duvalier himself. Not to mention the way the film is shot makes the viewer feel extremely complicit with the atrocities depicted, as we're being led by the characters as if we're VIPs on a guided tour. I couldn't finish this movie; it just felt so sickening in its intent, effects, and production history.

Excellent topic. Not trying to repeat movies already mentioned, but:
- The White Ribbon: We could choose any Haneke, but this one shows that evil does not come from only _one_ person. Which is correct and terrifying. 
- Antichrist: Again, we could choose any Von Trier movie, but the idea that Nature itself is a manifestation of evil is a topic that is not usually seen on films.
- Werckmeister Harmonies: I once read that the main song is the theme for the funeral of Humanity. Well fuck, that is such an accurate way to describe the entire movie.
- Speak No Evil: It might seem only akward at first, but then the masks fall off and the true spirit of Man emerges.
- Aniara (2018): This one is one of my favourite movies ever. We cannot talk about negative energy without mentioning it. It's not about the meaning of life, but it's about the _meaninglessness of existence_ . It's one of the most existentially depressing and pessimistic films I've ever seen, but when the credits roll we cannot help but to agree with it.
It is cruel. Kevin, specifically, is cruel. It is not a good time.

Vinterberg's *The Celebration* might be my favourite film. Absolutely incredible and oozing with visceral bad vibes. Genuinely, more people need to see this film - the first (and best) of the Dogme 95 movement. It got a lot of critical praise at release but I almost never see it brought up in film discourse online. I hate to say "underrated", especially considering the reception it had among scholars and critics, but it is absolutely underappreciated among contemporary film discussion circles.
Highly recommended giving into this movie with no pretext. Watched a couple weeks back and it was so refreshing.
